common_name: Moss Green Privet Honeysuckle (Compact Boxleaf Groundcover Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in humusy, well-drained soil; set plants on wide spacing and let the low, angular branching knit into a solid mat.

directions: Moss Green is a compact selection of privet honeysuckle, a boxleaf relative of the familiar vining honeysuckles that instead stays low and semi-evergreen, spreading far wider than it grows tall. Its dense, angular branching is set with small, glossy mid-green leaves, followed by inconspicuous spring flowers and translucent purple berries that songbirds favor into fall. Unlike most Lonicera, the species tolerates deep shade as readily as sun, making this selection useful as a shearable low hedge or filler mat beneath trees where little else holds a tidy evergreen line. Water during the first year to establish, then expect it to need only occasional shaping.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Blue Pearl Privet Honeysuckle (Translucent Blue-Berried Boxleaf Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in shade or sun; a few hours of sun improves autumn berry set.

directions: Blue Pearl was selected and named by UK plantsman Kevin Hobbs from seed-grown plants traced to material wild-collected in Guizhou, China, elevating what is normally grown as an anonymous dull hedging shrub into a garden-worthy specimen. Narrow, glossy dark green leaves clothe upright stems that perform well even in heavy shade, but the real draw is the autumn fruit: round, pale translucent-blue berries with the seeds visible through the skin, occasionally shading to mauve or clear. Grow in any well-drained soil and give it a little sun if a heavy berry display is the goal, otherwise treat it as a trouble-free shade filler. Light shaping after fruiting keeps the habit dense.

common_name: Cascade Carpet Salal (Dwarf Compact Evergreen Groundcover Salal)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath conifers or other shade trees.

directions: Cascade Carpet (US Plant Patent PP34,661) is a patented dwarf form of wild Pacific Northwest salal, discovered as a chance container seedling near Mission, BC in 2014 by grower Gurjit Sidhu and brought to market through Briggs Nursery. It runs at roughly half the height of the species while keeping salal's tough, glossy evergreen leaves and spring clusters of urn-shaped white flowers followed by edible blue-black berries. Its naturally low, dense habit suits a woodland groundcover role under Douglas fir and other acidic-soil shade where straight salal would quickly grow leggy and tall. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and avoid lime or heavy clay; established plantings need little water once rooted into native forest duff.

common_name: Cascade Sunrise Salal (Red New Growth Evergreen Salal)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; expect a taller habit in shade than in sun.

directions: Cascade Sunrise (US Plant Patent PP34,625) is a patented color selection of wild salal, discovered as a chance seedling of unrecorded parentage near Mission, BC in 2017 by grower Gurjit Sidhu and brought to market through Briggs Nursery, chosen for the bright red flush its new leaves show as they emerge before maturing to the species' usual glossy dark green. Narrower, more tapered foliage than wild salal sets off this new-growth color, and spring brings small pink urn-shaped flowers followed by summer berries that are edible and were historically a Pacific Northwest Indigenous food source. It grows taller and looser in shade than in sun, so give it understory space beneath conifers in acidic, humus-rich soil and let it naturalize as a woodland edge shrub.

common_name: Celtic Pride Siberian Cypress (Cold-Hardy Dry-Shade Groundcover Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; tolerates dry shade once roots are established.

directions: Celtic Pride (trademarked, US Plant Patent PP32,738) is a selection of Russia's sole native flat-sprayed conifer, bred for improved vigor and tip-dieback resistance over the species while extending reliable cold hardiness down to zone 2. Feathery, scale-like sprays lie flat like a soft-textured prostrate juniper, holding bright green through summer before shifting to bronze-purple for winter. It is among the few true conifers that performs reliably in dry, semi-shaded sites under deciduous canopy where most needled groundcovers fail from lack of light or summer drought. Give it sharp drainage at planting time; once established it needs almost no supplemental water or pruning.

common_name: Drew's Blue Siberian Cypress (Blue-Green Shade-Tolerant Carpet Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; forms a low, creeping carpet rather than a mound.

directions: Patented as 'Condrew' (US Plant Patent PP20,298) and sold as Drew's Blue, this selection of Siberian carpet cypress forms a low, creeping, generally prostrate mat of blue-green scale foliage that deepens to burgundy through winter and holds that color into spring. It is notably more shade-adapted than most needled groundcovers, thriving in partial to full shade where junipers and other prostrate conifers thin out. Slow-growing and long-lived, it needs little beyond sharp drainage at planting and is otherwise free of serious pests or disease. Use it to carpet a shaded slope or soften the base of taller shade shrubs.

common_name: Goldspot Siberian Cypress (Variegated Gold-Flecked Shade Groundcover Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil of any texture; part shade keeps gold flecking from scorching.

directions: Goldspot arose as a branch sport found by Allan Tate at Lime Cross Nursery in East Sussex, England, on an otherwise plain-green planting of Siberian cypress. Bright yellow fleck variegation runs through the green summer foliage year-round, intensifying against the purple-brown winter color typical of the species. It adapts to sand, silt, or clay as long as drainage is adequate and soil stays evenly moist, and its low, thick, spreading habit gives excellent urban tolerance and cold hardiness. Site it in part shade to keep the variegation from bleaching in hot afternoon sun.
